Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette: David Nguyen had been on foot patrol during a sweltering afternoon when the compound ambushed him. The heat had forced him to shed his outer gear earlier, and for a stretch, he had been standing exposed on the perimeter wall, the rough concrete scraping his shoulders and the sun beating down on his bare back. When the first mortars hit, the world collapsed into a cacophony of shelling, distant shouting, and the sudden, sharp crack of small arms. He remembered a low, guttural roar as a patrol motorcycle sped past the breach, its engine echoing off the tin roofs. There was no narrative in those first minutes, only a fragmented cascade of images, the thick smell of diesel and damp earth, and the stark vulnerability of having been completely naked in the triage tent where blankets had been ripped away to reach his wounds. He tried to describe it later, but the words kept slipping through his fingers. What remained was not a story he could tell, but a sequence of sensory fragments that refused to settle. The habits calcified over time. David stopped watching television and would step out of the room whenever the news aired footage of foreign conflict. He began to turn down requests to go out, finding that staying inside felt like the only way to conserve his energy. When his employer’s wellness program pushed for gym participation, he found reasons to stay home. These choices accumulated alongside his daily routines until his apartment became a space of carefully managed familiarity. Even inside his own home, however, David felt perpetually on guard. His software engineering work required long hours at his desk, staring at lines of code, but his attention never fully rested on the screen. He kept his blinds drawn, sat with his back to the wall, and scanned the hallway for sounds that could be mistaken for engines. At his desk, the silence sometimes betrayed him; a distant delivery van would rev, and his breath would catch until the sound faded. He began requesting permanent remote access, a shift his supervisors granted reluctantly, leaving him increasingly disconnected from his engineering team. David’s past did not stay buried. When he closed his eyes, memories arrived not as narratives but as relentless replays, rolling through his mind like a continuous film. He could still hear the specific whine of the motorcycle engine from that afternoon, a sound that would surface unbidden during debugging sessions or while making coffee. He could not put the event into words, but his body remembered the weight of it, and the sudden vulnerability of having been stripped of his gear and left exposed. Strangers approaching him, even to ask for directions or hand him a package, made his pulse spike and his shoulders lock. He was certain that stepping into an unreviewed space meant surrendering control to an unseen threat, and that proximity from an unknown person was never casual. His wife learned to speak softly and park her car three streets over, not out of disagreement, but because she knew a sudden footstep or a passing engine could pull him back. The sheer persistence of his symptoms had crossed a threshold. David had come to seek help because he no longer trusted his own capacity to navigate a world that felt permanently charged with danger. He was not looking for a cure so much as a way to lower the constant alarm in his chest, to sleep without scanning the dark, and to remember his deployment without feeling like he was back on that wall.
